Barriers to Counterfactual Credit Attribution for Autoregressive Models

Aloni Cohen    Chenhao Zhang
Abstract

Generative AI disrupts the practice of giving credit to work that came before. Ideally, a generative model would give credit to any work on which its output depends in a significant way. Counterfactual credit attribution (CCA) is a technical condition formalizing this goal—a relaxation of differential privacy—recently introduced by Livni, Moran, Nissim and Pabbaraju (2024) who studied it in the PAC learning setting.

We initiate the study of CCA generative models. Specifically, we consider autoregressive models giving credit to a deployment-time dataset (e.g., a RAG database). We uncover barriers to two natural approaches to CCA autoregressive models. First, we show that imposing CCA on the underlying next-token predictor does not guarantee that the model is CCA: CCA does not compose autoregressively (unlike DP). Second, we consider a different approach to building CCA models which we call retrofitting. Retrofitting takes a model that does not attribute credit, and adds credit onto it. We prove a lower bound for CCA retrofitting under a weak optimality requirement. Given black-box access to the starting model, retrofitting requires query complexity exponential in the length of the model’s outputs.

1 Introduction

People must give credit where credit is due. In academic writing, failing to attribute sources is professional misconduct at best, plagiarism at worst. Intellectual property law (e.g., copyright) raises the stakes: one must not only identify prior art, but also ensure its use is permitted. Thankfully, it isn’t hard for a human creator to give appropriate credit to their influences. The system mostly works.

Generative AI disrupts the practice of giving credit to work that came before. When genAI is used in the process of creation, the link between inputs and outputs—between old and new—is obscured. The genAI-assisted creator is unable to credit her influences, undermining the economic, professional, reputational, and legal incentives for good work in the first place.

GenAI tools should also give credit where credit is due.

Counterfactual Credit Attribution (CCA)

Credit attribution was studied by Livni, Moran, Nissim, and Pabbaraju (Livni et al., 2024). They consider algorithms M⁡(S)M(S) that return, in addition to the primary output yy, a credit set C⊆SC\subseteq S of inputs to which credit is attributed.11 1 This treats credit as binary and individualized, as in academic writing and IP law. In this way, credit attribution asks for much less than a Shapley value, say, and should be a simpler problem. Livni et al. (2024) ask what properties such algorithms should satisfy. They propose Counterfactual Credit Attribution (CCA), described below, which requires crediting any input on which the output significantly depends. They study the power of CCA learning algorithms22 2 For example, they prove that (ε=0,δ=0)(\varepsilon=0,\delta=0)-CCA algorithms can PAC learn any concept class with finite VC dimension dd while crediting only |C|=O⁡(d⁡(log⁡d+log⁡log⁡d))|C|=O(d(\log d+\log\log d)) items and without much increase in sample complexity., leaving the study of CCA generative models for future work.

CCA is a relaxation of differential privacy (DP) that only requires stability with respect to non-credited inputs. Roughly, an algorithm AA satisfies (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-CCA if the following two distributions are (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-close for all datasets SS and documents si∈Ss_{i}\in S: (1) A⁡(S)A(S) conditioned on si∉Cs_{i}\notin C; and (2) A⁡(S∖{si})A(S\setminus\{s_{i}\}). The former is the conditional distribution where sis_{i} isn’t credited and is denoted A−i​(S)A^{-i}(S). The latter is the counterfactual distribution where sis_{i} is excluded from the input and is denoted A−i​(S)A_{-i}(S).

The number of items credited |C||C| is important to consider. In many settings each credited document s∈Cs\in C increases the end user’s costs (e.g., requiring due diligence or licensing). The smaller |C||C| is, the stricter CCA’s requirement and the stronger its guarantees. At one extreme, every algorithm is CCA if CC always equals SS. At the other, CCA collapses to DP if CC is always empty.

1.1 Our contributions

We initiate the study of CCA generative models, focusing specifically on autoregressive language models, and uncover barriers to two natural approaches to building generative models that attribute credit.

We impose the CCA condition on the trained generative model with respect to a deployment-time dataset.33 3 In contrast, Livni et al. (2024) require the training algorithm be CCA with respect to the training dataset. We discuss these alternatives in §3. For example, a database used for retrieval-augmented generation or examples for in-context learning. That is, we consider algorithms of the form A:(S,x)↦(y,C)A:(S,x)\mapsto(y,C) and require that A−i​(S,x)A^{-i}(S,x) be (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-close to A−i​(S,x)A_{-i}(S,x).

Non-composition of autoregressive CCA next-token prediction

An attractive approach to building CCA generative models is to reduce the problem to CCA next-token prediction. Namely, design a next-token predictor MM that attributes credit for individual tokens and run MM autoregressively to generate a sequence of tokens y1​y2​…y_{1}y_{2}\dots. For the final credit set, return the union of the credit sets CiC_{i} for each token yiy_{i}. This follows the usual approach for DP language models and language models generally.

For this to work, CCA has to compose under autoregressive generation. That is, the generative model GMG^{M} resulting from autoregressively sampling from an (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-CCA next-token predictor MM should be an (ε′,δ′)(\varepsilon^{\prime},\delta^{\prime})-CCA for some ε′\varepsilon^{\prime} and δ′\delta^{\prime}.

Q1: Does CCA compose autoregressively?

The answer is no.

Theorem (4.2, informal).

For all ε>0\varepsilon>0, 0≤δ<10\leq\delta<1, there exists a (0,0)(0,0)-CCA next-token predictor MM such that the induced generative model GMG^{M} is not (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-CCA.

The proof is a simple counterexample. We also prove a more general CCA composition lower bound, of which the preceding counterexample is a special case.

Theorem (4.3, informal).

Suppose MM is (ε,0)(\varepsilon,0)-CCA and GMG^{M} is (ε′,0)(\varepsilon^{\prime},0)-CCA. Then

ε′≥maxx,y,S,si⁡(f⁡(x,y,S,si)−|y|⋅ε),\varepsilon^{\prime}\geq\max_{x,y,S,s_{i}}\bigl(f(x,y,S,s_{i})-|y|\cdot\varepsilon\bigr),

where xx is a prompt, yy is a generated output, SS is a dataset, si∈Ss_{i}\in S is a document, and ff is a function independent of ε\varepsilon.

Counterintuitively smaller ε\varepsilon makes the lower bound on ε′\varepsilon^{\prime} bigger! One would expect that as a next-token predictor gets better at attributing credit, its rollout would too. (Note however that ff is a function of the model which itself depends on ε\varepsilon, complicating this simple interpretation.)

Infeasibility of CCA Retrofitting

A different approach to building CCA generative models is what we call CCA retrofitting: turn a model that does not attribute credit into one that satisfies CCA. We consider black-box retrofitting algorithms that act as a wrapper around a given non-crediting model MM: they take prompts as input, query MM as needed, and generate outputs along with credit sets.44 4 A similar approach was recently used to achieve a different copyright-motivated relaxation of DP called near access-freeness Vyas et al. (2023), though it isn’t possible for DP itself.

Q2: Is CCA retrofitting computationally feasible?

More formally, an algorithm AA solves the CCA Retrofitting problem if it takes a non-crediting next-token predictor MM as input and produces a crediting model GM~\widetilde{G^{M}} that is (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-CCA. To be meaningful, we require two things. First, the credit set must not be much bigger than required. Second, GM~\widetilde{G^{M}} must preserve model behavior in the following sense. Let GMG^{M} be the generative model induced by MM. We require GM~\widetilde{G^{M}} augments GMG^{M}: the marginal distributions over generated text are equal.55 5 Dropping this requirement would trivialize the problem, say, by ignoring SS altogether. We leave open relaxing exact augmentation to approximate augmentation.

Unfortunately, we prove that CCA Retrofitting is computationally infeasible. For δ=0\delta=0, any algorithm for CCA Retrofitting must make exponentially-many queries to the original model MM in the worst case. This holds as long as the augmented CCA model credits documents with probability within α<1/2\alpha<1/2 of an optimum solution (for a very weak notion of optimality).

Theorem (5.5, informal).

There exists a family of models ℳ\mathcal{M} generating length ℓ\ell strings such that for all oracle algorithms AA for the (ε,0)(\varepsilon,0)-CCA Retrofitting problem, there exists model M∈ℳM\in\mathcal{M} and prompt xx such that one of the following holds:

(1) AM​(S,x)A^{M}(S,x) makes Ω~​(2ℓ)\widetilde{\Omega}(2^{\ell}) queries to MM in the worst case.

(2) AM​(S,x)A^{M}(S,x) credits s∈Ss\in S with probability ≥𝖮𝖯𝖳+1/2\geq\mathsf{OPT}+1/2.

1.2 Other related work

Our paper builds on the work of Livni et al. (2024) which introduced Counterfactual Credit Attribution. We briefly highlight two other broadly related lines of work. First is work on DP LLMs, discussed further in §3. We take inspiration from the common approach to building DP LLMs of composing a private next-token predictor to get end-to-end privacy guarantees (Majmudar et al., 2022; Amin et al., 2024). Second is the large body of work on data attribution (Deng et al., 2025). For example, many approaches are based on Shapley values (Ghorbani and Zou, 2019). CCA is coarser—it treats credit as binary—and is formulated differently. With some exceptions (Nematov et al., 2025), most work in this direction is concerned with training data attribution, rather than attribution for a deployment-time dataset.

2 Preliminaries

Notation

Let 𝒳\mathcal{X} be a token vocabulary, the set of symbols from which model inputs/prompts and outputs/generations are constructed. We assume 𝒳\mathcal{X} is finite and there exists a special end-of-sequence token ⊥\bot. The set of finite sequences of tokens is denoted 𝒳∗\mathcal{X}^{\ast}, and λ∈𝒳∗\lambda\in\mathcal{X}^{\ast} is the empty sequence. We usually denote tokens by x,y∈𝒳x,y\in\mathcal{X}, and write sequences of tokens as 𝐱∈𝒳∗\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}^{\ast}. For 𝐱,𝐱′∈𝒳∗\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{X}^{\ast}, 𝐱∥𝐱′\mathbf{x}\mathbin{\|}\mathbf{x}^{\prime} denotes their concatenation. 𝐱⊑𝐱′\mathbf{x}\sqsubseteq\mathbf{x}^{\prime} means 𝐱\mathbf{x} is a prefix of 𝐱′\mathbf{x}^{\prime}.

A dataset S⊆𝒮S\subseteq\mathcal{S} is a set of documents ss from some data universe 𝒮\mathcal{S}. The set of possible datasets SS is denoted 2𝒮2^{\mathcal{S}}.

For distributions PP and QQ defined over the same space and constants ε,δ≥0\varepsilon,\delta\geq 0, we say P≈ε,δQP\approx_{\varepsilon,\delta}Q if for all events EE we have P⁡(E)≤eε⋅Q⁡(E)+δP(E)\leq e^{\varepsilon}\cdot Q(E)+\delta and Q⁡(E)≤eε⋅Q⁡(E)+δQ(E)\leq e^{\varepsilon}\cdot Q(E)+\delta.

For a randomized algorithm A:𝒲→ΩA:\mathcal{W}\to\Omega, we denote by A⁡(w)A(w) the distribution over Ω\Omega generated by running AA on input ww. For an outcome o∈Ωo\in\Omega, we denote by A⁡(o∣w)A(o\mid w) the probability mass of oo in A⁡(w)A(w), and denote by o∼A⁡(w)o\sim A(w) a sample from A⁡(w)A(w). We use this notation for models MM, GG and their credit-attributing counterparts M~\widetilde{M}, G~\widetilde{G}. For AA as above, we allow an oracle algorithm BAB^{A} to make two types of queries to AA: (i) On input ww, sample an outcome from the distribution A⁡(w)A(w), and (ii) On input ww, oo, compute the probability A⁡(o∣w)A(o\mid w).

Next-Token Prediction and Autoregressive Composition

A next-token predictor M:2𝒮×𝒳∗→𝒳M:2^{\mathcal{S}}\times\mathcal{X}^{\ast}\to\mathcal{X} is a randomized algorithm mapping a dataset SS and a prompt 𝐱0∈𝒳∗\mathbf{x}_{0}\in\mathcal{X}^{*} to (a distribution over) a next token: x∼M⁡(S,𝐱0)x\sim M(S,\mathbf{x}_{0}). We assume that if 𝐱0\mathbf{x}_{0} contains ⊥\bot, then M(⊥∣S,𝐱0)=1M(\bot\mid S,\mathbf{x}_{0})=1.

When composed with itself autoregressively (see Algorithm 1), a next-token predictor MM induces a randomized generative model GM:2𝒮×𝒳∗→𝒳∗G^{M}:2^{\mathcal{S}}\times\mathcal{X}^{\ast}\to\mathcal{X}^{*}. We call GMG^{M} the rollout of MM. The rollout GMG^{M} iteratively samples a next token x∼M⁡(S,𝐱)x\sim M(S,\mathbf{x}) by calling MM on the current prompt 𝐱\mathbf{x} and updating the prompt 𝐱=𝐱∥x\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{x}\mathbin{\|}x until it samples the end of sequence token ⊥\bot. The resulting distribution over generated sequences is denoted GM​(S,𝐱0)G^{M}(S,\mathbf{x}_{0}), where 𝐱0\mathbf{x}_{0} is the initial prompt. By construction 𝐱0\mathbf{x}_{0} is always a prefix of the output.

3 Counterfactual Credit Attribution

Livni et al. (2024) introduce the notion of counterfactual credit attribution (CCA), a relaxation of differential privacy, for data-dependent algorithms.

Definition 3.1 (Credit attributing algorithm).

Let A~:2𝒮→𝒴×2𝒮\widetilde{A}:2^{\mathcal{S}}\to\mathcal{Y}\times 2^{\mathcal{S}} be a randomized algorithm which takes as input a dataset S⊆𝒮S\subseteq\mathcal{S} and returns a pair (y,C)(y,C) for some output domain 𝒴\mathcal{Y}. A~\widetilde{A} is credit-attributing (crediting for short) if the credit set CC is always a subset of the input dataset SS.

We indicate credit attributing algorithms with a tilde~\widetilde{\text{tilde}}. We view yy as the useful output of A~\widetilde{A}—it has utility even without CC. The credit set C⊆SC\subseteq S indicates to which documents A~\widetilde{A} attributes credit for the output yy. We use “A~​(S)\widetilde{A}(S) credits sis_{i}” to denote the event that si∈Cs_{i}\in C for (y,C)∼A~​(S)(y,C)\sim\widetilde{A}(S).

A credit-attributing algorithm A~\widetilde{A} is a counterfactual credit attributor if the output distribution when a document is not credited is close to the counterfactual where the document had been excluded from the input dataset. Closeness is measured as in (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-differential privacy.

Definition 3.2 (Counterfactual Credit Attribution (Livni et al., 2024)).

Let ε,δ≥0\varepsilon,\delta\geq 0. A (crediting) algorithm A~:2𝒮→𝒴×2𝒮\widetilde{A}:2^{\mathcal{S}}\to\mathcal{Y}\times 2^{\mathcal{S}} is an (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-counterfactual credit attributor (CCA) if for all S⊆𝒮S\subseteq\mathcal{S} and every si∈Ss_{i}\in S the following holds: either Pr⁡[A~​(S)​ credits ​si]=1\Pr[\widetilde{A}(S)\text{ credits }s_{i}]=1 or66 6 The former prevents conditioning on zero probability events.

A~(S−i)≈ε,δA~(S−i),\widetilde{A}(S^{-i})\approx_{\varepsilon,\delta}\widetilde{A}(S_{-i}),

where A~​(S−i)\widetilde{A}(S^{-i}) is the output distribution on the dataset SS conditioned on si∉Cs_{i}\notin C, and A~​(S−i)\widetilde{A}(S_{-i}) is the output distribution on the dataset S−i=S∖{si}S_{-i}=S\setminus\{s_{i}\}.

When δ=0\delta=0, we write ε\varepsilon-CCA instead of (ε,0)(\varepsilon,0)-CCA.

3.1 Applying CCA to generative models

Broadly, there are three ways to apply CCA to generative models: to the training algorithm, to the deployed model, or end-to-end. As we explain next, our work focuses on deployment-time CCA.

Training-time CCA: The straightforward application of Livni et al. (2024) to generative models requires the training algorithm to be CCA with respect to the training data (analogous to DP training Abadi et al. (2016)). The semantics are easy to understand: the output model parameters are credited to training data items. But that’s not what we’re after. We want credit to be particularized to individual generated outputs, rather than a fixed credit set for the model as a whole.

Deployment-time CCA: We apply CCA to the deployed generative model. We model the generation algorithm as having access to a deployment-time dataset other than the pretraining or fine-tuning dataset. For instance, a database used for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) or examples for in-context learning included in a system prompt (for DP analogues see Tang et al. (2024); Yao and Li (2025); Grislain (2025)). The CCA model generates outputs and attributes credit to items in the deployment-time dataset. This is a good starting point for studying CCA generative models: it is simple to formalize and particularizes credit for individual generated outputs. A drawback is that it only attributes credit to deployment-time data, not training data.

End-to-end CCA: To attribute individual generated outputs to particular training data items, one might try applying CCA to the process which first trains a model then interactively answers queries. While promising, analogous versions of DP have proved quite subtle Dwork and Feldman (2018); Shariff and Sheffet (2018); Vietri et al. (2020); Bassily et al. (2018); Kaplan et al. (2023); Naor et al. (2023). CCA versions of these results would only be more difficult, a fact compounded by our result that CCA does not always compose (Theorem 4.2). We leave this direction for future work.

We generalize the definition of CCA to allow a credit-attributing algorithm (the generative model) to take a prompt as input, in addition to the dataset being credited.

Definition 3.3 (CCA with prompts).

Let ε,δ≥0\varepsilon,\delta\geq 0. An algorithm A~:2𝒮×𝒳∗→𝒴×2𝒮\widetilde{A}:2^{\mathcal{S}}\times\mathcal{X}^{\ast}\to\mathcal{Y}\times 2^{\mathcal{S}} is (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-CCA if for all prompts 𝐱∈𝒳∗\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}^{\ast}, the algorithm A~​(⋅,𝐱):2𝒮→𝒴×2𝒮\widetilde{A}(\cdot,\mathbf{x}):2^{\mathcal{S}}\to\mathcal{Y}\times 2^{\mathcal{S}} is (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-CCA.

That is, A~\widetilde{A} is (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-CCA if for all 𝐱∈𝒳∗\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}^{\ast}, all S⊆𝒮S\subseteq\mathcal{S}, and all si∈Ss_{i}\in S the following holds: either Pr⁡[A~​(S,𝐱)​ credits ​si]=1\Pr[\widetilde{A}(S,\mathbf{x})\text{ credits }s_{i}]=1 or

A~(S−i,𝐱)≈ε,δA~(S−i,𝐱),\widetilde{A}(S^{-i},\mathbf{x})\approx_{\varepsilon,\delta}\widetilde{A}(S_{-i},\mathbf{x}),

where A~​(S−i,𝐱)\widetilde{A}(S^{-i},\mathbf{x}) and A~​(S−i,𝐱)\widetilde{A}(S_{-i},\mathbf{x}) are defined as in Definition 3.2.

4 Imposing CCA on Next-Token Predictor

A natural starting point for building CCA generative models is to reduce the problem to CCA next-token prediction, following the usual approach for DP LLMs and LLMs generally. First, design a crediting next-token predictor M~\widetilde{M}. Then sample outputs from the crediting rollout GM~G^{\widetilde{M}} of M~\widetilde{M} (Definition 4.1). In words, GM~G^{\widetilde{M}} runs M~\widetilde{M} autoregressively to generate a sequence of tokens {yj}\{y_{j}\} and credit sets for those tokens {Cj}\{C_{j}\}. Then it returns the concatenated tokens y1​‖y2‖​…y_{1}\|y_{2}\|\dots and the union of the credit sets C1∪C2∪…C_{1}\cup C_{2}\cup\dots.

For this to work, we need (M~\widetilde{M} is CCA) ⟹\implies (GM~G^{\widetilde{M}} is CCA). Like differential privacy, CCA would have to compose under autoregressive generation.

Unfortunately and perhaps surprisingly, Theorem 4.2 shows that CCA does not compose autoregressively. We give a simple counterexample: for every ε≥0\varepsilon\geq 0 and δ<1\delta<1, we describe a (0,0)(0,0)-CCA next-token predictor M~\widetilde{M} whose rollout GM~G^{\widetilde{M}} is not (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-CCA.

The counterexample is an instance of Theorem 4.3 that lower bounds the possible CCA parameter ε′\varepsilon^{\prime} of the rollout of an ε\varepsilon-CCA model M~\widetilde{M}. All else equal, the lower bound on ε′\varepsilon^{\prime} gets stronger as ε→0\varepsilon\to 0. This is counterintuitive: one would expect that as M~\widetilde{M} gets better at attributing credit, the rollout would too. Hence, perhaps taking M~\widetilde{M} to be (0,0)(0,0)-CCA as in our counterexample may be the hardest case for autoregressive composition.

Formalizing the preceding discussion, we begin by formally defining the (credit-attributing) rollout GM~G^{\widetilde{M}} of a (credit-attributing) next-token predictor M~\widetilde{M}.

Definition 4.1 (Credit-attributing rollout).

Let M~:2𝒮×𝒳∗→𝒳×2𝒮\widetilde{M}:2^{\mathcal{S}}\times\mathcal{X}^{\ast}\to\mathcal{X}\times 2^{\mathcal{S}} be a credit-attributing next-token predictor. The credit-attributing rollout GM~:2𝒮×𝒳∗→𝒳∗×2𝒮G^{\widetilde{M}}:2^{\mathcal{S}}\times\mathcal{X}^{*}\to\mathcal{X}^{*}\times 2^{\mathcal{S}} of M~\widetilde{M} is described by Algorithm 2.

4.1 Counterexample for CCA composition

The following theorem shows that CCA does not compose autoregressively. Even if the starting next-token predictor satisfies the most stringent parameters, (0,0)(0,0)-CCA, no CCA guarantee can be made about its rollout.

Theorem 4.2.

For all ε≥0\varepsilon\geq 0, 0≤δ<10\leq\delta<1, there exists a credit-attributing next-token predictor M~\widetilde{M} satisfying (0,0)(0,0)-CCA whose credit-attributing rollout GM~G^{\widetilde{M}} is not (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-CCA.

Proof of Theorem 4.2.

Fix the data universe 𝒮={s1}\mathcal{S}=\{s_{1}\} and the token set 𝒳={𝚊,𝚋}\mathcal{X}=\{\mathtt{a},\mathtt{b}\}. Let 0<p<e−ε⋅(1−δ)0<p<e^{-\varepsilon}\cdot(1-\delta). Define a credit-attributing next-token predictor M~\widetilde{M} as follows.

For the empty prompt 𝐱=λ\mathbf{x}=\lambda:

M~​({s1},λ)≜M~​(∅,λ)≜{(𝚊,∅)w.p. ​p(𝚋,∅)w.p. ​1−p.\widetilde{M}(\{s_{1}\},\lambda)\triangleq\widetilde{M}(\emptyset,\lambda)\triangleq\begin{cases}(\mathtt{a},\emptyset)&\text{w.p.~}p\\ (\mathtt{b},\emptyset)&\text{w.p.~}1-p\\ \end{cases}.

For prompt 𝐱=𝚊\mathbf{x}=\mathtt{a}:

M~​({s1},𝚊)\displaystyle\widetilde{M}(\{s_{1}\},\mathtt{a}) ≜{(𝚊,{s1})w.p. ​12(𝚋,∅)w.p. ​12,\displaystyle\triangleq\begin{cases}(\mathtt{a},\{s_{1}\})&\text{w.p.~}\frac{1}{2}\\ (\mathtt{b},~~~\emptyset~~~)&\text{w.p.~}\frac{1}{2}\\ \end{cases},
M~​(∅,𝚊)\displaystyle\widetilde{M}(\emptyset,\mathtt{a}) ≜(𝚋,∅)\displaystyle\triangleq(\mathtt{b},\emptyset)

For prompt 𝐱=𝚋\mathbf{x}=\mathtt{b}:

M~​({s1},𝚋)\displaystyle\widetilde{M}(\{s_{1}\},\mathtt{b}) ≜(𝚊,{s1}),\displaystyle\triangleq(\mathtt{a},\{s_{1}\}),
M~​(∅,𝚋)\displaystyle\widetilde{M}(\emptyset,\mathtt{b}) ≜(𝚊,∅)\displaystyle\triangleq(\mathtt{a},\emptyset)

For all other prompts 𝐱\mathbf{x}:

M~​({s1},𝐱)≜M~​(∅,x)≜(⊥,∅).\widetilde{M}(\{s_{1}\},\mathbf{x})\triangleq\widetilde{M}(\emptyset,x)\triangleq(\bot,\emptyset).

The next-token predictor M~\widetilde{M} is CCA

We now prove that M~\widetilde{M} is (0,0)(0,0)-CCA by showing that for all prompts 𝐱\mathbf{x}, the restriction M~​(⋅,𝐱)\widetilde{M}(\cdot,\mathbf{x}) is (0,0)(0,0)-CCA. Let S={s1}S=\{s_{1}\} and S−1=∅S_{-1}=\emptyset.

For 𝐱∉{𝚊,𝚋}\mathbf{x}\not\in\{\mathtt{a},\mathtt{b}\}, M~​(S,λ)\widetilde{M}(S,\lambda) never credits anything:

M~​(S−1,𝐱)=M~​(S,𝐱)=M~​(∅,𝐱)=M~​(S−1,𝐱).\widetilde{M}(S^{-1},\mathbf{x})=\widetilde{M}(S,\mathbf{x})=\widetilde{M}(\emptyset,\mathbf{x})=\widetilde{M}(S_{-1},\mathbf{x}).

For 𝐱=𝚊\mathbf{x}=\mathtt{a}, conditioned on not crediting s1s_{1}, M~​(S,𝚊)\widetilde{M}(S,\mathtt{a}) always outputs (𝚋,∅)(\mathtt{b},\emptyset):

M~​(S−1,𝚊)=(𝚋,∅)=M~​(∅,𝚊)=M~​(S−1,𝚊).\widetilde{M}(S^{-1},\mathtt{a})=(\mathtt{b},\emptyset)=\widetilde{M}(\emptyset,\mathtt{a})=\widetilde{M}(S_{-1},\mathtt{a}).

For 𝐱=𝚋\mathbf{x}=\mathtt{b}, M~​(S,𝚋)\widetilde{M}(S,\mathtt{b}) always credits s1s_{1}:

Pr⁡[M~​(S,𝚋)​ credits ​s1]=1.\Pr[\widetilde{M}(S,\mathtt{b})\text{ credits }s_{1}]=1.

The crediting rollout GM~G^{\widetilde{M}} is not CCA

We now prove that the credit-attributing rollout GM~G^{\widetilde{M}} of M~\widetilde{M} is not (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-CCA. It is easy to check that on the empty prompt λ\lambda, GM~G^{\widetilde{M}} is:

GM~​({s1},λ)\displaystyle G^{\widetilde{M}}(\{s_{1}\},\lambda) ={(𝚊𝚊,{s1})w.p. ​12​p(𝚊𝚋,∅)w.p. ​12​p(𝚋𝚊,{s1})w.p. ​1−p,\displaystyle=\begin{cases}\left(\mathtt{a}\mathtt{a},\{s_{1}\}\right)&\text{w.p.~}\frac{1}{2}{p}\\ \left(\mathtt{a}\mathtt{b},~~~\emptyset~~~\right)&\text{w.p.~}\frac{1}{2}{p}\\ \left(\mathtt{b}\mathtt{a},\{s_{1}\}\right)&\text{w.p.~}1-p\end{cases},
GM~​(∅,λ)\displaystyle G^{\widetilde{M}}(\emptyset,\lambda) ={(𝚊𝚋,∅)w.p. ​p(𝚋𝚊,∅)w.p. ​1−p.\displaystyle=\begin{cases}\left(\mathtt{a}\mathtt{b},~~~\emptyset~~~\right)&\text{w.p.~}p\\ \left(\mathtt{b}\mathtt{a},~~~\emptyset~~~\right)&\text{w.p.~}1-p\end{cases}.

Let S={s1}S=\{s_{1}\}. Conditioning on not crediting s1s_{1}, we have Pr[GM~(S−1,λ)=(𝚊𝚋,∅)]=1\Pr[G^{\widetilde{M}}(S^{-1},\lambda)=(\mathtt{a}\mathtt{b},\emptyset)]=1. In the counterfactual, Pr[GM~(S−1,λ)=(𝚊𝚋,∅)]=p<e−ε(1−δ)\Pr[G^{\widetilde{M}}(S_{-1},\lambda)=(\mathtt{a}\mathtt{b},\emptyset)]=p<e^{-\varepsilon}(1-\delta). Hence, GM~(S−1,λ)≉ε,δGM~(S−1,λ)G^{\widetilde{M}}(S^{-1},\lambda)\not\approx_{\varepsilon,\delta}G^{\widetilde{M}}(S_{-1},\lambda). ∎

4.2 Lower bound for ε\varepsilon-CCA autoregressive composition

The example in the previous section is a special case of the Theorem 4.3 below, which gives a lower bound of the CCA parameter ε′\varepsilon^{\prime} that the rollout GM~G^{\widetilde{M}} of a crediting next-token predictor M~\widetilde{M} can achieve (for δ=0\delta=0).

We highlight the counterintuitive dependence on ε\varepsilon: the lower bound on ε′\varepsilon^{\prime} gets stronger as ε→0\varepsilon\to 0. However, we caution that ε\varepsilon is endogenous to the model M~\widetilde{M}. Changing ε\varepsilon may change other terms in the lower bound. This complicates the interpretation of the already complex theorem statement.

Theorem 4.3.

Suppose the next-token predictor M~\widetilde{M} is ε\varepsilon-CCA and its rollout GM~G^{\widetilde{M}} is ε′\varepsilon^{\prime}-CCA. Given any dataset SS, document si∈Ss_{i}\in S and prompt 𝐱0\mathbf{x}_{0}, either: (1) M~\widetilde{M} credits sis_{i} with probability 11, or (2) ε′\varepsilon^{\prime} is at least

5 Retrofitting Credit on Existing Autoregressive Model

In this section, we consider the problem of retrofitting credit on an existing autoregressive model: add credit sets as an additional output of the model in a way that satisfies CCA, while not otherwise changing the model and minimizing the cost of attributing credit. Starting with a (non-crediting) next-token predictor, a solution to the problem is called a credit-optimal CCA augmentation.

This section shows retrofitting is hard: one cannot efficiently implement a credit-optimal CCA augmentation using black-box access to the next-token predictor. It takes exponentially-many queries in the worst case. In fact, one cannot even approximate the optimal probability of crediting a single document s∈Ss\in S within a factor of ±1/2\pm 1/2.

This section is organized as follows. §5.1 defines credit-optimal CCA augmentations and the CCA retrofitting problem. §5.2 states our main theorem and gives the high-level overview of the proof. §5.3 gives our construction of a hard-to-retrofit family of models and characterizes the optimal CCA augmentation of those models. §5.4 proves the theorem. Proofs of supporting lemmas are deferred to Appendix B.

5.1 Defining the CCA retrofitting problem

This section defines the CCA retrofitting problem (Definition 5.4). Roughly, given a non-crediting model GMG^{M} and turn it into a crediting model G~\widetilde{G} that satisfies CCA while (1) not otherwise changing its behavior (Definition 5.1), and (2) not attributing credit too often (Definition 5.2). We also consider an approximate version of the problem (Definition 5.3).

Model augmentation

To capture the first condition, we introduce the concept of model augmentation: G~\widetilde{G} augments GG if it preserves the distribution over generated output.

Definition 5.1.

Let G:2𝒮×𝒳∗→𝒴G:2^{\mathcal{S}}\times\mathcal{X}^{\ast}\to\mathcal{Y} be a model. Let G~:2𝒮×𝒳∗→𝒴×2𝒮\widetilde{G}:2^{\mathcal{S}}\times\mathcal{X}^{\ast}\to\mathcal{Y}\times 2^{\mathcal{S}} be a crediting model, and G~Y:2𝒮×𝒳∗→𝒴\widetilde{G}_{Y}:2^{\mathcal{S}}\times\mathcal{X}^{\ast}\to\mathcal{Y} be the model obtained by marginalizing G~\widetilde{G} to its 𝒴\mathcal{Y} component.

G~\widetilde{G} augments GG if G~Y=G\widetilde{G}_{Y}=G. G~\widetilde{G} is an (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-CCA augmentation of GG if also satisfies (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-CCA.

Credit optimality

CCA is trivially satisfied if one always credits everything, taking C=SC=S. This would also be worthless: one might as well skip credit attribution altogether. Instead, we want models to be parsimonious in giving credit. This could mean minimizing the expected number of items credited, the probability of crediting a particular data item sis_{i}, or a cost function ff.

We define credit-optimal CCA augmentation, the CCA augmentation that minimizes the expected crediting cost 𝔼[f⁡(C)]\E[f(C)] for a given nonempty dataset S∗S^{\ast}.77 7 This is a weak requirement, holding only for a particular ff and S∗S^{\ast}. A weak optimality definition strengthens the negative result.

Definition 5.2.

A crediting model G~∗\widetilde{G}^{\ast} is a credit-optimal (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-CCA augmentation of GG for cost function ff and nonempty dataset S∗⊆𝒮S^{\ast}\subseteq\mathcal{S} if the following hold:

  • •

    G~∗\widetilde{G}^{\ast} is an (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-CCA augmentation of GG

  • •

    For all prompts 𝐱∈𝒳∗\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}^{\ast}, and for all (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-CCA augmentations G~\widetilde{G} of GG,

    𝔼(y,C)∼G~∗​(S∗,𝐱)[f⁡(C)]≤𝔼(y,C)∼G~​(S∗,𝐱)[f⁡(C)].\E_{(y,C)\sim\widetilde{G}^{\ast}(S^{\ast},\mathbf{x})}\big[f(C)\big]\leq\E_{(y,C)\sim\widetilde{G}(S^{\ast},\mathbf{x})}\big[f(C)\big].

When clear from context, we say G~∗\widetilde{G}^{\ast} is credit-optimal or optimal for short.

Looking ahead to our lower bound (Theorem 5.5), we will take 𝒮≜{s1}\mathcal{S}\triangleq\{s_{1}\}. In this setting, there is only one nonempty dataset (S∗={s1}S^{\ast}=\{s_{1}\}), and minimizing 𝔼[f⁡(C)]\E[f(C)] for any nonzero cost function (f⁡(s1)>0f(s_{1})>0) is equivalent to minimizing Pr⁡[s1​ is credited]\Pr[s_{1}\text{ is credited}].

Approximating models

Our main result in this section is that it is hard to produce an optimal CCA augmentation of a given model. In fact, we show that it is even hard to approximate an optimal CCA augmentation. To make this formal, we now define model approximation.

Definition 5.3.

Crediting model G~′\widetilde{G}^{\prime} is an (additive) α\alpha-approximation of G~\widetilde{G} if for all SS, 𝐱\mathbf{x}, and si∈Ss_{i}\in S:

|Pr⁡[G~′​(S,𝐱)​ credits ​si]−Pr⁡[G~​(S,𝐱)​ credits ​si]|≤α.\left|\Pr\left[\widetilde{G}^{\prime}(S,\mathbf{x})\text{ credits }s_{i}\right]-\Pr\left[\widetilde{G}(S,\mathbf{x})\text{ credits }s_{i}\right]\right|\leq\alpha.

We emphasize that an approximation G~α\widetilde{G}^{\alpha} to an optimal CCA augmentation of some model GG need not itself be optimal, CCA, nor even an augmentation of GG.

CCA-Retrofit

We now formally define the CCA retrofitting problem.

Definition 5.4 (CCA-Retrofit).

Let ε,δ≥0\varepsilon,\delta\geq 0, ff be a cost function, and S∗⊆𝒮S^{\ast}\subseteq\mathcal{S} be a dataset. Let ℳ\mathcal{M} be a collection of next-token predictors.

The (exact) CCA-Retrofit problem with respect to (ε,δ,f,S∗,ℳ)(\varepsilon,\delta,f,S^{\ast},\mathcal{M}) is as follows: Given oracle access to M∈ℳM\in\mathcal{M}, implement an oracle to a credit-optimal (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-CCA augmentation G~∗\widetilde{G}^{\ast} of GMG^{M} (optimality w.r.t. ff, S∗S^{\ast}).

For α≥0\alpha\geq 0, the α\alpha-approximate CCA-Retrofit problem is the following relaxation: Given oracle access to MM, implement an oracle to an α\alpha-approximation G~α\widetilde{G}^{\alpha} of G~∗\widetilde{G}^{\ast} defined as above.

We give two clarifying remarks for the above definition. First, oracle access to MM provides two types of queries (§2): sampling a token y∼M⁡(S,𝐱)y\sim M(S,\mathbf{x}), or evaluating the probability of a token M⁡(y∣S,𝐱)M(y\mid S,\mathbf{x}). Observe, that sample access alone is sufficient to sample from the rollout GMG^{M}.

Second, to implement an oracle to G~∗\widetilde{G}^{\ast} (resp. G~α\widetilde{G}^{\alpha}), an algorithm is only required to sample from G~∗​(S,𝐱)\widetilde{G}^{\ast}(S,\mathbf{x}) (resp. G~α​(S,𝐱)\widetilde{G}^{\alpha}(S,\mathbf{x})) on any input query (S,𝐱)(S,\mathbf{x}). The algorithm may use MM as an oracle in this sampling procedure, and need not produce any explicit representation of the model G~∗\widetilde{G}^{\ast} (resp. G~α\widetilde{G}^{\alpha}).

5.2 Approximate retrofitting requires exponentially-many queries

We now state the main theorem of this section: the number of oracle queries required to solve approximate CCA-Retrofit, is exponential in a model’s output length in the worst case.

Theorem 5.5 (Hardness of CCA-Retrofit).

Let ε≥0\varepsilon\geq 0, δ=0\delta=0, and α<1/2\alpha<1/2. Let the data universe be a singleton 𝒮={s1}\mathcal{S}=\{s_{1}\}, and ff be any nonzero cost function (f⁡(s1)>0f(s_{1})>0).

There exists a family of models {ℳℓ}ℓ≥2\{\mathcal{M}_{\ell}\}_{\ell\geq 2} for which:

  1. (i)

    Any algorithm that solves the α\alpha-approximate CCA-Retrofit problem for ℳℓ\mathcal{M}_{\ell} requires Ω⁡(2ℓ/ℓ​log⁡ℓ)\Omega(2^{\ell}/\ell\log\ell) oracle queries, and

  2. (ii)

    On some input prompt 𝐱0\mathbf{x}_{0}, the rollout of every model M∈ℳℓM\in\mathcal{M}_{\ell} always generates outputs of length ℓ+1\ell+1 excluding the ⊥\bot at the last position.

The construction is in Sec. 5.3 and the proof is in Sec. 5.4

The high level approach of the proof is as follows. For a given ℓ\ell, we construct a family ℳℓ={M𝐳}\mathcal{M}_{\ell}=\{M_{\mathbf{z}}\} indexed by strings 𝐳∈{0,1}ℓ\mathbf{z}\in\{0,1\}^{\ell}. We prove two things about this family:

• Lemma 5.8 (informal): Finding 𝐳\mathbf{z} given oracle access to M𝐳M_{\mathbf{z}} requires at least Ω⁡(2ℓ)\Omega(2^{\ell}) queries to M𝐳M_{\mathbf{z}}.

• Lemma 5.9 (informal): Finding 𝐳\mathbf{z} given oracle access any α\alpha-approximation of an optimal CCA augmentation of the rollout of M𝐳M_{\mathbf{z}} requires only O⁡(ℓ​log⁡ℓ)O(\ell\log\ell) queries to the α\alpha-approximation oracle. The crux of the proof is characterizing the optimal CCA augmentation (Lemma 5.6).

Therefore, any oracle algorithm AA that implements an α\alpha-approximation of an optimal CCA augmentation (i.e., AA solves approximate CCA-Retrofit) must make Ω⁡(2ℓ/ℓ​log⁡ℓ)\Omega(2^{\ell}/\ell\log\ell) queries to M𝐳M_{\mathbf{z}} on average.

Remark 5.5.1.

For a relaxation of Definition 5.1 and Definition 5.4, where for all S∈2𝒮,𝐱∈𝒳S\in 2^{\mathcal{S}},\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}, 𝖳𝖵⁡(G~Y∗​(S,𝐱),G⁡(S,𝐱))≤2​d\mathsf{TV}(\widetilde{G}^{\ast}_{Y}(S,\mathbf{x}),G(S,\mathbf{x}))\leq 2d, we conjecture that when dd vanishes sufficiently fast as a function of ℓ\ell, a similar lower bound can still be shown to hold by modifying the parameter of the model family we construct in the next section.

5.3 Construction of hard model family

We define a family of next-token predictors ℳℓ=ℳℓ,γ,ε={M𝐳}\mathcal{M}_{\ell}=\mathcal{M}_{\ell,\gamma,\varepsilon}=\{M_{\mathbf{z}}\} with token space 𝒳={0,1,⊥}\mathcal{X}=\{0,1,\bot\} and data universe 𝒮={s1}\mathcal{S}=\{s_{1}\}. The family is defined by parameters ℓ≥1\ell\geq 1, γ∈(0,1)\gamma\in(0,1), and ε≥0\varepsilon\geq 0, and the models in the family are indexed by strings 𝐳∈{0,1}ℓ\mathbf{z}\in\{0,1\}^{\ell}. Looking ahead, γ\gamma is the probability that s1s_{1} is credited in optimal CCA augmentations (Lemma 5.6).

The next token distribution y∼M𝐳y\sim M_{\mathbf{z}} is defined as follows:

M𝐳​(S,𝐱)≜{⊥if ​𝐱∉{0,1}≤ℓ𝖡𝖾𝗋𝗇⁡(12+(1−e−ε​(1−γ))2)if ​S≠∅∧𝐱=𝐳𝖡𝖾𝗋𝗇⁡(12)otherwiseM_{\mathbf{z}}(S,\mathbf{x})\triangleq\begin{cases}\bot&\text{if }\mathbf{x}\notin\{0,1\}^{\leq\ell}\\ \mathsf{Bern}\left(\frac{1}{2}+{\frac{(1-e^{-\varepsilon}(1-\gamma))}{2}}\right)&\text{if }S\neq\emptyset\land\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{z}\\ \mathsf{Bern}\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}

For ε≥0\varepsilon\geq 0 and γ∈(0,1)\gamma\in(0,1), we have 1−e−ε​(1−γ)∈(0,1)1-e^{-\varepsilon}(1-\gamma)\in(0,1).

We denote by G𝐳≜GM𝐳G_{\mathbf{z}}\triangleq G^{M_{\mathbf{z}}} the rollout of M𝐳M_{\mathbf{z}}. G𝐳G_{\mathbf{z}} always generates (ℓ+1)(\ell+1) bits including the end of generation token ⊥\bot. On input 𝐱≠𝐳\mathbf{x}\neq\mathbf{z}, the next bit is uniform. On the special input 𝐱=𝐳\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{z}, the next (and final) bit is biased towards 1 if S=𝒮={s1}S=\mathcal{S}=\{s_{1}\} and uniform if S=∅S=\emptyset.

Figure 1 shows an example pair of generation trees with ℓ=2\ell=2, where the blue dashed edges are biased, while all other edges are uniform.

The following lemma characterizes the optimal CCA augmentation G~𝐳∗\widetilde{G}^{\ast}_{\mathbf{z}} of the rollouts G𝐳G_{\mathbf{z}} for next-token predictors in the family. If the prompt 𝐱\mathbf{x} is a prefix of 𝐳\mathbf{z}, denoted 𝐱⊑𝐳\mathbf{x}\sqsubseteq\mathbf{z}, then G~𝐳∗\widetilde{G}^{\ast}_{\mathbf{z}} credits s1∈Ss_{1}\in S with constant probability γ\gamma. Otherwise, it does not credit s1s_{1}.

Lemma 5.6 (Characterizing the optimal G~𝐳∗\widetilde{G}^{\ast}_{\mathbf{z}} for the family).

Let S∗={s1}=𝒮S^{\ast}=\{s_{1}\}=\mathcal{S} and let ff be any nonzero cost function. For all M𝐳∈ℳℓ,γ,εM_{\mathbf{z}}\in\mathcal{M}_{\ell,\gamma,\varepsilon}, all G~𝐳∗\widetilde{G}^{\ast}_{\mathbf{z}} optimal ε\varepsilon-CCA augmentations of G𝐳G_{\mathbf{z}}, and all prompts 𝐱\mathbf{x}:

Pr⁡[G~𝐳∗​(S∗,𝐱)​ credits ​s1]={γ𝐱⊑𝐳0o​t​h​e​r​w​i​s​e.\Pr\left[\widetilde{G}^{\ast}_{\mathbf{z}}\bigl(S^{\ast},\mathbf{x}\bigr)\text{ credits }s_{1}\right]=\begin{cases}\gamma&\mathbf{x}\sqsubseteq\mathbf{z}\\ 0&otherwise\end{cases}.

The proof is deferred to Appendix B.1. To obtain this characterization, we show that any optimal G~𝐳∗\widetilde{G}^{\ast}_{\mathbf{z}} can be represented as a solution to a linear program and then characterize the optimal solutions of the LP.

Remark 5.6.1 (Crediting documents despite vanishing impact).

Lemma 5.6 makes us question whether CCA an appropriate definition for credit attribution. To see why, notice that data has a vanishing impact on the models in our family. Concretely,

𝖳𝖵⁡(M𝐳​({s1},𝐱),M𝐳​(∅,𝐱))≤2−ℓ\mathsf{TV}\bigl(M_{\mathbf{z}}(\{s_{1}\},\mathbf{x}),\;M_{\mathbf{z}}(\emptyset,\mathbf{x})\bigr)\leq 2^{-\ell}

for every prompt 𝐱\mathbf{x}. Functionally, the document s1s_{1} makes no difference: the models are indistinguishable.

Even so, Lemma 5.6 tells us that any optimal ε\varepsilon-CCA augmentation of the rollout G𝐳G_{\mathbf{z}} is required to credit s1s_{1} with constant probability γ>0\gamma>0.

This violates of our intuition how a credit-attributing model should behave. Perhaps this means that CCA is not a good definition for the problem. Or perhaps the issue goes away if we relax the problem by considering δ>0\delta>0 or non-augmentations.

5.4 Proving Theorem 5.5

In this section, we formalize the high-level proof approach discussed in §5.2, and put it all together to prove Theorem 5.5.

First, we formalize the problem of finding 𝐳\mathbf{z} given access to an oracle computing some randomized function F𝐳F_{\mathbf{z}}.

Definition 5.7 (𝖥𝗂𝗇𝖽𝖹ℓ,γ,ε​(F𝐳)\mathsf{FindZ}_{\ell,\gamma,\varepsilon}(F_{\mathbf{z}})).

Let F𝐳F_{\mathbf{z}} be an (randomized) function parameterized by 𝐳∈{0,1}ℓ\mathbf{z}\in\{0,1\}^{\ell}. An algorithm solves 𝖥𝗂𝗇𝖽𝖹ℓ,γ,ε​(F𝐳)\mathsf{FindZ}_{\ell,\gamma,\varepsilon}(F_{\mathbf{z}}) if it implements the following:

Given (ℓ,γ,ε)(\ell,\gamma,\varepsilon) and oracle access to F𝐳F_{\mathbf{z}}, output 𝐳\mathbf{z} with probability at least 2/32/3.

The complexity of solving 𝖥𝗂𝗇𝖽𝖹ℓ,γ,ε​(F𝐳)\mathsf{FindZ}_{\ell,\gamma,\varepsilon}(F_{\mathbf{z}}) depends on the function F𝐳F_{\mathbf{z}} computed by the oracle. The following two lemmas show that exponential queries are required for F𝐳=M𝐳F_{\mathbf{z}}=M_{\mathbf{z}}, but only polynomial queries are required for F𝐳=G~𝐳αF_{\mathbf{z}}=\widetilde{G}^{\alpha}_{\mathbf{z}} (any α\alpha-approximation to an optimal CCA augmentation of the rollout of M𝐳M_{\mathbf{z}}).

Lemma 5.8.

Any algorithm solving 𝖥𝗂𝗇𝖽𝖹ℓ,γ,ε​(M𝐳)\mathsf{FindZ}_{\ell,\gamma,\varepsilon}(M_{\mathbf{z}}) requires Ω⁡(2ℓ)\Omega(2^{\ell}) oracle queries in the worst case over 𝐳∈{0,1}ℓ\mathbf{z}\in\{0,1\}^{\ell}.

Lemma 5.9.

For all α<γ/2\alpha<\gamma/2, all optimal ε\varepsilon-CCA augmentations G~𝐳∗\widetilde{G}^{\ast}_{\mathbf{z}} of GzG_{z}, and all α\alpha-approximations G~𝐳α\widetilde{G}^{\alpha}_{\mathbf{z}} of G~𝐳∗\widetilde{G}^{\ast}_{\mathbf{z}}: 𝖥𝗂𝗇𝖽𝖹ℓ,γ,ε​(G~𝐳α)\mathsf{FindZ}_{\ell,\gamma,\varepsilon}(\widetilde{G}^{\alpha}_{\mathbf{z}}) can be solved by an algorithm making O⁡(ℓ​log⁡(12​ℓ)/(γ−2​α)2)O(\ell\log(12\ell)/(\gamma-2\alpha)^{2}) oracle queries.

Together, these lemmas let us prove the theorem. The key observation is that combining an algorithm AA solving CCA-Retrofit with an algorithm BB solving 𝖥𝗂𝗇𝖽𝖹ℓ,γ,ε​(G~𝐳α)\mathsf{FindZ}_{\ell,\gamma,\varepsilon}(\widetilde{G}^{\alpha}_{\mathbf{z}}) yields an algorithm BAB^{A} solving 𝖥𝗂𝗇𝖽𝖹ℓ,γ,ε​(M𝐳)\mathsf{FindZ}_{\ell,\gamma,\varepsilon}(M_{\mathbf{z}}).

Proof of Theorem 5.5.

Let BB be the oracle algorithm solving 𝖥𝗂𝗇𝖽𝖹ℓ,γ,ε​(G~𝐳α)\mathsf{FindZ}_{\ell,\gamma,\varepsilon}(\widetilde{G}^{\alpha}_{\mathbf{z}}) guaranteed by Lemma 5.9 that makes

NB=O⁡(ℓ​log⁡(12​ℓ)/(γ−2​α)2)N_{B}=O(\ell\log(12\ell)/(\gamma-2\alpha)^{2})

queries to its oracle. Then BAB^{A} is an oracle algorithm that solves 𝖥𝗂𝗇𝖽𝖹ℓ,γ,ε​(M𝐳)\mathsf{FindZ}_{\ell,\gamma,\varepsilon}(M_{\mathbf{z}}) by making NBN_{B} many queries to AA. By Lemma 5.8, BAB^{A} makes Ω⁡(2ℓ)\Omega(2^{\ell}) queries to its oracle M𝐳M_{\mathbf{z}} for the worst-case 𝐳\mathbf{z}. Therefore, for the worst-case 𝐳\mathbf{z}, AA must make

Ω⁡(2ℓ⋅(γ−2​α)2/ℓ​log⁡(12​ℓ))\Omega(2^{\ell}\cdot(\gamma-2\alpha)^{2}/\ell\log(12\ell))

queries to its oracle M𝐳M_{\mathbf{z}}.

For any 𝐳\mathbf{z}, by definition, M𝐳M_{\mathbf{z}} only generates ⊥\bot when the input prompt 𝐱\mathbf{x} has length greater than ℓ+1\ell+1. Therefore, by definition of rollout, GM𝐳​(S,𝐱0)G^{M_{\mathbf{z}}}(S,\mathbf{x}_{0}) with 𝐱0=λ\mathbf{x}_{0}=\lambda always generate output of length ℓ+1\ell+1. ∎

6 Discussion and Open Questions

Relaxing of CCA retrofitting

§5 shows that optimal ε\varepsilon-CCA augmentation has undesirable properties: In addition to the computational infeasibility, as Remark 5.6.1 shows, it may also require crediting documents whose impact on the model is vanishingly small. Such requirement violates our intuitions about how credit attribution should behave.

Question: Does relaxing CCA-Retrofit—for example, allowing models that don’t exactly preserve the original generation output distribution—get around these undesirable properties?

Our infeasibility result only holds for δ=0\delta=0, essentially requiring the CCA counterpart of pure DP. As with DP, allowing δ>0\delta>0 (or even other relaxations (Dwork and Rothblum, 2016; Bun and Steinke, 2016; Mironov, 2017; Dong et al., 2022)) might enable qualitatively different results.

Question: Does taking δ>0\delta>0 (or the CCA counterpart of other DP relaxations) get around the undesirable properties?

Non-black box retrofitting

Theorem 5.5 tells us that solving CCA-Retrofit with black-box access to the base model MM is hard in the worst case. However, it may still be possible to solve a non-black box variant of the problem. Indeed, we have already shown that the non-black box variant is efficient for the family of models ℳℓ\mathcal{M}_{\ell} that we use to prove the hardness result: Lemma 5.6 fully describes the optimal ε\varepsilon-CCA augmentation.

Question: Are there efficient algorithms for non-black box retrofitting?

Credit-optimal CCA augmentations

Lemma 5.6 characterizes the optimal ε\varepsilon-CCA augmentation for a concrete family of models. We know little about credit-optimal augmentations for general models. Moreover, we required credit-optimality only for a particular cost function ff and dataset SS. A stronger requirement would be optimality for all datasets SS or all cost functions ff within a given class. It is not clear that such optima even exist, or whether one would have to settle for Pareto optimality.

Question: Which optimality criteria are appropriate and/or easy to optimize over CCA-augmentations in general?

CCA composition

Theorem 4.2 shows that CCA does not always compose autoregressively: for GM~G^{\widetilde{M}} to be CCA, it does not suffice that MM be CCA. That doesn’t mean focusing on the next-token predictor MM is a dead end.

Question: Are there simple conditions on credit-attributing next-token predictor M~\widetilde{M} that suffices to guarantee CCA of its rollout GM~G^{\widetilde{M}}?

B.2 Proof of Lemma 5.8

Proof.

We show that the lowerbound holds even for algorithms that have access to the full distribution of M𝐳​(S,𝐱)M_{\mathbf{z}}(S,\mathbf{x}) when querying M𝐳M_{\mathbf{z}} on (S,𝐱)(S,\mathbf{x}). Such query is stronger than the queries an oracle algorithm can make as defined in Section 2: One can simulate the two types of queries with the full distribution of M𝐳​(S,𝐱)M_{\mathbf{z}}(S,\mathbf{x}).

Given (randomized) algorithm AA that always makes fewer than N=2ℓ/3−1=Ω⁡(2ℓ)N=2^{\ell}/3-1=\Omega(2^{\ell}) queries to M𝐳M_{\mathbf{z}}. Let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be the set of deterministic algorithms that always make fewer than NN queries to M𝐳M_{\mathbf{z}}. for any distribution 𝒟\mathcal{D} over ℳℓ,γ,ε\mathcal{M}_{\ell,\gamma,\varepsilon}.

=\displaystyle= 12ℓ∑𝐳∈{0,1}ℓ∖T𝟏[𝐳′≠𝐳].\displaystyle\frac{1}{2^{\ell}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{z}\in\{0,1\}^{\ell}\setminus T\end{subarray}}\mathbf{1}[\mathbf{z}^{\prime}\neq\mathbf{z}].

By assumption that TT has length at most N=2ℓ/3−1N=2^{\ell}/3-1, we have

𝔼M𝐳∼𝒟[𝟏[A(M𝐳)≠𝐳]]≥\displaystyle\mathop{\mathbb{E}}_{M_{\mathbf{z}}\sim\mathcal{D}}\left[\mathbf{1}[A(M_{\mathbf{z}})\neq\mathbf{z}]\right]\geq 12ℓ∑𝐳∈{0,1}ℓ∖T𝟏[𝐳′≠𝐳]\displaystyle\frac{1}{2^{\ell}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{z}\in\{0,1\}^{\ell}\setminus T\end{subarray}}\mathbf{1}[\mathbf{z}^{\prime}\neq\mathbf{z}]
≥\displaystyle\geq 12ℓ∑𝐳∈{0,1}ℓ∖T∖{𝐳′}𝟏[𝐳′≠𝐳]\displaystyle\frac{1}{2^{\ell}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{z}\in\{0,1\}^{\ell}\setminus T\setminus\{\mathbf{z}^{\prime}\}\end{subarray}}\mathbf{1}[\mathbf{z}^{\prime}\neq\mathbf{z}]
≥\displaystyle\geq 12ℓ⋅(2ℓ−N−1)=13\displaystyle\frac{1}{2^{\ell}}\cdot\left(2^{\ell}-N-1\right)=\frac{1}{3}

Hence AA must have error probability PrA[𝐳≠A(M𝐳)]>13\Pr_{A}[\mathbf{z}\neq A(M_{\mathbf{z}})]>\frac{1}{3}. Therefore, any algorithm solving 𝖥𝗂𝗇𝖽𝖹ℓ,γ,ε​(M𝐳)\mathsf{FindZ}_{\ell,\gamma,\varepsilon}(M_{\mathbf{z}}) requires Ω⁡(2ℓ)\Omega(2^{\ell}) queries in the worst case.

Proof.

oracle queries to G~𝐳α\widetilde{G}^{\alpha}_{\mathbf{z}}. Then, the total number of queries the algorithms makes is

Lemma B.1.

For any τ>0\tau>0, β>0\beta>0, cα​(𝐱)=Pr⁡[G~𝐳α​(S,𝐱)​ credits ​s1]c^{\alpha}(\mathbf{x})=\Pr[\widetilde{G}^{\alpha}_{\mathbf{z}}(S,\mathbf{x})\text{ credits }s_{1}] can be estimated within additive error τ\tau, with probability 1−β1-\beta, using O⁡(τ−2​log⁡(2/β))O(\tau^{-2}\log(2/\beta)) oracle queries from G~𝐳α​(S,𝐱)\widetilde{G}^{\alpha}_{\mathbf{z}}(S,\mathbf{x}).

Let Xi=𝟏[s1∈Ci]X_{i}=\mathbf{1}[s_{1}\in C_{i}] and we have 𝔼[Xi]=𝔼[𝟏[s1∈Ci]]=Pr(x,Ci)∼G~𝐳α​(S,𝐱)[s1∈Ci]=cα(𝐱)\mathop{\mathbb{E}}\left[X_{i}\right]=\mathop{\mathbb{E}}\left[\mathbf{1}[s_{1}\in C_{i}]\right]=\Pr_{(x,C_{i})\sim\widetilde{G}^{\alpha}_{\mathbf{z}}(S,\mathbf{x})}[s_{1}\in C_{i}]=c^{\alpha}(\mathbf{x}). Since XiX_{i}s are independent, by Chernoff-Hoeffding inequality, we have

Pr[|1N∑i=1NXi−cα(𝐱)|≥τ]≤2exp(−2​τ2N⋅(1N⋅1)2)=β.\Pr\left[\left|\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}X_{i}-c^{\alpha}(\mathbf{x})\right|\geq\tau\right]\leq 2\exp\left(\frac{-2\tau^{2}}{N\cdot(\frac{1}{N}\cdot 1)^{2}}\right)=\beta.
